item.title: Salt marshes are proving to be powerful allies in building a climate-resilient coastline
item.description: Salt marsh sediment and vegetation can remain largely intact even during extreme storm surges. This was demonstrated in a large-scale experiment in which researchers transported sections of salt marsh to an experimental facility capable of producing the world's largest artificial waves. The results show how salt marshes can contribute to natural coastal protection, both in the Netherlands and beyond. The results were published in the journals Nature and Communications Sustainability. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: ¿Por qué las mujeres siguen infrarrepresentadas en el Congreso de EE. UU.?

También analizamos el informe de FIFPRO sobre las desigualdades salariales y los problemas de salud mental en el fútbol femenino, y el debate abierto en Colombia por un proyecto de ley que busca reformular la educación sexual con un enfoque biológico. Tres escenarios distintos en los que la igualdad sigue en disputa. Fuente: France 24 - Español.

item.title: Reconstructing 16,000 years of summer temperature change in the Western Balkans
item.description: Researchers at Eötvös Loránd University (ELTE) have reconstructed approximately 16,000 years of summer temperature changes from sediments collected at Lake Prokoško in Bosnia and Herzegovina. The findings show how the Western Balkans responded to rapid climate changes at the end of the last glacial period, how warmer and cooler phases unfolded during the Holocene, and how the impact of human land use became increasingly pronounced. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Methane emissions in Baltimore show seasonal, daily trends
item.description: Natural gas leaks are a significant source of methane emissions in cities, but it can be hard to pinpoint exactly where and why they happen. And methane, a potent greenhouse gas that is the main chemical component of natural gas, has been historically undercounted or omitted in emissions estimates, according to a team of atmospheric and climate science researchers in the Penn State College of Earth and Mineral Sciences. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Africa's bats could survive climate change—if they can find somewhere to live
item.description: Climate change and changes in the way land is used are the two biggest threats to wildlife because they change the environment in which animals survive and thrive. Knowing how species respond to these pressures is central to planning conservation actions. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Seabird guano and native trees keep islands above rising seas: Study
item.description: Low-lying tropical atoll islands appear remarkably vulnerable to climate change. But when shrouded with native forests and with abundant seabird populations, these islands may keep up with rising sea levels, a new study finds. Seabirds act as biological pumps, moving nutrients from feeding areas in the open ocean to roosting and nesting areas on land […] Fuente: Mongabay.

item.title: How life on Earth experiences climate change
item.description: Climate change can look very different at the scale of a forest, field or hillside. A new review shows how changes in vegetation and atmospheric conditions can cause local microclimates to warm at very different rates from the regional climate—and why this matters for understanding how biodiversity will respond to climate change. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: World set to breach 1.5°C warming limit set by Paris Climate Agreement
item.description: The UN is warning that global commitments to cut planet-heating emissions are falling far short of the Paris climate goals of 1.5 degrees Celsius warming – and put the world on course for 2.6C warming this century. The report by the United Nations Environment Programme lays bare the chasm between rhetoric and action when it comes to tackling global warming, and the challenge before political leaders at November's COP31 climate summit - set to take place next month in Turkey. Story by Emerald Maxwell. Fuente: France 24 - English.
